subtype: Approach: weigh job security against integrity in a values list [Thinking]
passage:
"You've been staring at that page for an hour," said Jomon's brother, Sachin, setting down two teacups.

"It's a list. Left side: my salary, the loan instalment, Amma's medicines. Right side: my name, the risk if the audit catches it, and whether I can look at myself."

"What did the manager ask, exactly?"

"To mark the delivery as received before the truck even came. I'd be signing a false line."

"And the left side?"

"Heavy. But if I sign and it comes out, I lose the job anyway, and my name with it."

"So?"

"So I say no tomorrow. And tonight I update my CV, just in case." Jomon tore his page in half and set the CV half on the laptop.

qa.q: What did the manager ask Jomon to do?
qa.a: To mark the delivery as received before the truck even came.

qa.q: What is Jomon feeling as he weighs the two sides of the list?
qa.a: Jomon feels torn and anxious about the salary and loan on one side, but the list leaves him more certain that his self-respect and name matter too.

qa.q: What could Jomon say to the manager to make the refusal easier to hear, and why?
qa.a: Jomon could offer to record the delivery honestly on the day it arrives, because it meets the manager's need for an accurate record without a false line.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Jomon's plan to refuse and update the CV?
qa.a: Sachin may feel relieved and proud that Jomon is not acting rashly, since the CV shows the refusal comes with a backup.

grounding: An employee lists what is at stake on each side, decides to refuse, and prepares a job-market backup.

subtype: Approach: weigh job security against integrity in a values list [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Joseph. Two weeks ago my manager, Yusuf, asked me to sign off a safety test report for a batch of water pumps that hadn't finished testing. 'The client is shouting. Sign it, we'll test next week.'
I didn't answer that day. That night I split a sheet of paper into two columns.
If I sign: I keep my job for now, my ₹9,000 education-loan EMI stays easy, Yusuf stays happy. But my name is on a false report. If a pump fails, that's legal trouble with my signature on it. And I'd know what I did every time I saw that client's name.
If I refuse: maybe a bad appraisal, or worse. The EMI gets scary. But my name stays clean, and I can look at myself.
Seeing it all at once, the answer wasn't hard. The fear was.
So the next morning I told Yusuf I couldn't sign until testing was done, and emailed the quality team that the batch was still untested. That same weekend, I updated my CV and messaged three classmates about openings. Just in case.

qa.q: What does 'The fear was' tell you about how Joseph felt?
qa.a: Joseph was clear about what was right, but still frightened of losing the job and struggling with the EMI.

qa.q: What else could Joseph do to make refusing safer?
qa.a: Keep a dated note of Yusuf's request, and know whom to contact in HR if the pressure continues.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Joseph's refusal?
qa.a: Yusuf may be annoyed with the client shouting, but now cannot claim not to have been told the batch was untested.

grounding: Shows an employee listing salary, loan, reputation, legal risk and self-respect on each side, refusing to sign, and preparing a job-market backup.

subtype: Approach: weigh job security against integrity in a values list [Thinking]
passage:
Mentor's note, 6 February. Kalyani, women-in-engineering mentoring circle.
Shreya brought me a dilemma today. Her site supervisor has asked her to sign a materials register saying a cement delivery was tested when it wasn't. She is afraid of saying no; her family counts on her salary, and she has an education loan.
I suggested she write down what she stands to gain and lose either way, and she did it at my table. Signing: keeps the job for now, keeps the peace, pays the EMI. But her name on a false register, possible legal liability if a structure fails, and, she wrote, 'I won't respect myself.' Refusing: risk of a poor review or losing the job. But a clean record, no legal exposure, self-respect.
She looked at the list a long time. 'The job side is scary. The other side is permanent.'
She has decided to refuse, and to tell the quality engineer today that the delivery still needs testing. She will also start applying elsewhere quietly. I'll check in with her on Friday.

qa.q: What was Shreya asked to sign?
qa.a: A materials register saying a cement delivery was tested when it wasn't.

qa.q: What does 'The job side is scary. The other side is permanent' reveal about Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya is afraid for her job and family, but more deeply unwilling to carry a lasting stain on her record and self-respect.

qa.q: What else could support Shreya after refusing?
qa.a: A written record of the request, and a talk with HR or a senior if the supervisor retaliates, while the job search continues.

qa.q: How does the dilemma look to Kalyani, the mentor who wrote the note?
qa.a: Kalyani helps Shreya see the whole picture without deciding for her, and plans a Friday check-in.

grounding: Shows an employee listing job security, loan, legal risk and self-respect on each side, choosing to refuse and quietly preparing other options.
